I will keep it simple and plant what I know best on the land I can still manage steadily myself: winter wheat followed by summer maize. In Quzhou County, this two-crop rotation fits the climate, the irrigation habits, and the machines I can easily hire or use. At my age, I do not want to take big market or management risks with vegetables, cotton, or other crops that need more labor and closer technical work. Winter wheat gives me a stable crop that is already in the ground at the start of the season, and after harvest I can quickly sow summer maize, which is reliable and suits our heat and rainfall pattern.

For management, I will not chase extreme yields. I will aim for stable output and controlled cost. On wheat, I will topdress nitrogen once around jointing, water when it matters most, and spray only when disease, aphids, or weeds are really a threat. I will use improved seed and normal rotary tillage because it is familiar and practical for me. After wheat harvest, I will return to the field quickly and plant summer maize with hybrid seed for stronger yield stability. I will fertilize maize a bit heavier on nitrogen than wheat, keep phosphorus and potassium moderate, irrigate only a few times depending on rain, and do a limited number of pesticide applications mainly for weeds and common insects. My main decision is stability: fewer crops, one familiar rotation, moderate inputs, and work I know I can finish well.
